newsitem.title: USA: Airlines won't predict merger impact.
newsitem.headline: Airlines won't predict merger impact.

text.p: Major U.S. airlines said Sunday it was too early to forecast the impact of the proposed $13.3 billion merger between Boeing Co. and McDonnell Douglas Corp. on aircraft prices or their airplane-buying strategies.
"It is too early to tell," Delta Air Lines Inc. spokesman Todd Clay said. "It is like looking into a crystal ball to tell what would be coming down the pipeline."

Seattle, Wash.-based Boeing and McDonnell Douglas, based in St. Louis, announced plans to merge via a stock swap, creating what they said would be the largest integrated aerospace company in the world.
"We'll have to see what transpires," Northwest Airlines Corp. spokesman Jon Austin said. "It's a long way from announcing a deal to consummating it."
Boeing and McDonnell Douglas said they expected the deal to close by mid-1997, but it was subject to approval by shareholders of both companies and certain regulatory agencies.
Continental Airlines Inc., AMR Corp. and USAir Group Inc. declined to comment on the planned merger, while UAL Corp., Chicago-based parent company of United Airlines, was not immediately available.

Trans World Airlines Inc. spokesman Mark Abels noted that TWA was a customer of both aircraft manufacturers. "Both of these manufacturers make good aircraft, and we have aircraft on order from both," he said.

Trans World Airlines had 20 firm orders and 20 optional orders placed with Boeing for its 757 carrier, he said. "These are not all purchase orders -- some of them are leased, but they are all new aircraft."
Abels said TWA also had 15 MD-80 Series aircraft on order from McDonnell Douglas.
Southwest Airlines Co., whose entire fleet is comprised of 243 Boeing 737 jets, said it continued to be a strong supporter of Boeing aircraft.
"In October 1997, we will be the launch customer for Boeing's 737-700 aircraft," Southwest spokesman Ginger Hardage said.
